profile.feeling: The plain “I” — often left out, because the verb already says who is speaking.

senses.def: the ego, the self (as a noun: الْأَنَا)

examples.tr: I am a student — and you?

examples.text: أَنَا أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ، أَمَّا هُوَ فَيُحِبُّ الشَّايَ.
examples.tr: I like coffee, whereas he likes tea.
The book talks about the self and the other.

profile.synonymsNone: No other independent “I”; as object or possessor Arabic uses the suffixes ـنِي / ـي (forms, not synonyms).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanāku; cognate with Hebrew אֲנִי (aní) and Amharic እኔ (enē); compare Egyptian jnk (Coptic ⲁⲛⲟⲕ, anok).

funFacts: The noun الْأَنَا, “the ego”, is a semantic loan from German “das Ich” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Written with a final alif, but in connected MSA speech the last vowel is short: ʾana. The alif is pronounced long only at a pause.
The pronoun is not needed with a verb: آكُلُ alone already means “I eat”.
subtleties: أَنَا before a verb adds emphasis or contrast: أَنَا آكُلُ = it is I who eat (not someone else).

profile.feeling: Direct and everyday — used even with strangers; politeness comes from titles, not from the pronoun.

senses.def: you (one man; masculine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: You are my friend. (to a man)
Where are you from? (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: lit. “your presence” — a polite way to address a man, very common in Egypt; grammatically a noun with a suffix, not a pronoun

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanta (Wiktionary); Hebrew אַתָּה (atá) continues the same form with the n assimilated.

funFacts: The -ta of أَنْتَ is the same ending as in the past verb: كَتَبْتَ, “you (m.) wrote”.
pitfalls: أَنْتَ (man) and أَنْتِ (woman) are the same letters, انت; only the final vowel differs (-ta / -ti). In unvocalized text only the context tells you.
With أَنْتَ the present verb starts with تَـ and has no ending: أَنْتَ تَأْكُلُ — the same form as “she eats” (هِيَ تَأْكُلُ).
subtleties: Arabic has no built-in polite “you” like German Sie or Russian вы: respect is shown with titles and formulas (حَضْرَتُكَ, يَا أُسْتَاذُ).

profile.feeling: The same everyday “you”, addressed to one woman.

senses.def: you (one woman; feminine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: You are my friend. (to a woman)
Where are you from? (to a woman)

synonyms.nuance: lit. “your presence” — polite address to a woman, very common in Egypt; a noun with a suffix, not a pronoun

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔanti (Wiktionary); compare the Hebrew feminine אַתְּ (at).

funFacts: Hebrew lost the n in אַתְּ (at); Arabic keeps it: ʾanti.
pitfalls: The verb after أَنْتِ ends in -īna: أَنْتِ تَأْكُلِينَ, تَشْرَبِينَ — not تَأْكُلُ.
Same letters as أَنْتَ (انت): only the kasra (-ti) shows that a woman is meant.
subtleties: Adjectives agree too: أَنْتِ جَاهِزَةٌ (to a woman) vs أَنْتَ جَاهِزٌ (to a man).

profile.feeling: Neutral; also “it” for every masculine thing.

senses.def: he (third person masculine singular subject pronoun)
it (referring to a masculine noun, also a thing)

examples.tr: The book? It is on the table.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُوَ is the only third-person masculine singular subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـهُ).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šuʔa (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הוּא (hu).

funFacts: Psychology’s “id” is الْهُوَ in Arabic — a calque of Freud’s German “Es” (Wiktionary), just as الْأَنَا is “das Ich”.
pitfalls: هُوَ also means “it” for masculine nouns: الْبَصَلُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا = the onions? They (lit. it) are here. Do not always translate “he”.
subtleties: Between a subject and a definite predicate, هُوَ / هِيَ can act like a copula (ḍamīr al-faṣl): الْمُشْكِلَةُ هِيَ الْوَقْتُ = the problem is time.

profile.feeling: Neutral; also “it” for feminine things — and “they” for non-human plurals.

senses.def: she (third person feminine singular subject pronoun)

examples.tr: The car? It is in front of the house.
The books? They are on the table.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هِيَ is the only third-person feminine singular subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـهَا).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šiʔa (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הִיא (hi).

funFacts: Hebrew הִיא (hi) is the same Semitic word.
pitfalls: Non-human plurals are referred to with هِيَ, not هُمْ: الْجَزَرَاتُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا = the carrots? They are here.
subtleties: The verb after هِيَ starts with تَـ, like the verb after أَنْتَ: هِيَ تَأْكُلُ / أَنْتَ تَأْكُلُ.

profile.feeling: Togetherness: family, team, “us”.

senses.def: we (first person plural subject pronoun; also for two people)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: نَحْنُ is the only first-person plural subject pronoun (as object or possessor: the suffix ـنَا).

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *niḥnu; cognate with Hebrew אֲנַחְנוּ (anáchnu).

funFacts: The same n appears in the suffix “us/our”: بَيْتُنَا (our house), عِنْدَنَا (we have).
pitfalls: The final -u is fixed: نَحْنُ never changes with case.
The present verb with نَحْنُ starts with نَـ: نَأْكُلُ، نَشْرَبُ، نُحِبُّ.
subtleties: Used for men, women and mixed groups, and also for two people: Arabic has no dual “we”.

profile.feeling: Addressing a group — a class, a family, friends; men or a mixed group.

senses.def: you (several people: men, or a mixed group) — masculine plural

profile.synonymsNone: No other word. For a group of women only: أَنْتُنَّ; for exactly two people: the dual أَنْتُمَا.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔantum; cognate with Hebrew אַתֶּם (atém).

funFacts: Hebrew אַתֶּם (atém) is the same word: Hebrew assimilated the n (*ʔantum → attem), Arabic kept it.
pitfalls: One man in a group of women is enough for أَنْتُمْ; only an all-female group is أَنْتُنَّ.
Exactly two people are addressed with the dual أَنْتُمَا (ʾantumā), not with أَنْتُمْ.
subtleties: There is no fixed polite “you” like German Sie or Russian вы; formal letters sometimes address one important person with the plural (-كُمْ: حَضْرَتُكُمْ), but that is style, not a rule.

profile.feeling: Addressing a group of women or girls only.
profile.synonymsNone: No other word; a mixed group is أَنْتُمْ, two women أَنْتُمَا.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔantin; Hebrew has the same pair אַתֶּם / אַתֶּן.

funFacts: Hebrew אַתֶּן (atén) is its counterpart: both languages keep a separate “you” for a group of women.
pitfalls: Write the šadda: أَنْتُنَّ (antunna), with a doubled n.
Most spoken dialects have lost this form and say أَنْتُو / إِنْتُو to everybody; in MSA keep أَنْتُنَّ for women only.
subtleties: Its verb forms have their own ending -tunna / -na: كُنْتُنَّ (you women were).

profile.feeling: A group of people — men, or men and women together.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُنَّ is its feminine counterpart (only women), and هُمَا is for exactly two.

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šum (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew הֵם (hem).

funFacts: For exactly two people Arabic uses the dual هُمَا — a living dual that Hebrew pronouns no longer have.
pitfalls: A mixed group takes هُمْ: one man among women is enough for the masculine.
Not for things: non-human plurals are هِيَ (الْبَصَلَاتُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا).
subtleties: When هُمْ comes first, the verb agrees fully (هُمْ يَأْكُلُونَ); a noun subject after the verb leaves the verb singular (يَأْكُلُ الطُّلَّابُ).

profile.feeling: A group of women only.

senses.def: they (feminine plural, a group of women)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: هُمْ is the masculine/mixed counterpart.

etymology.text: Feminine plural of the inherited Semitic third-person pronoun series (هُوَ، هِيَ، هُمْ، هُنَّ); Hebrew הֵן (hen) is the corresponding form.
etymology.src: Arabic and Hebrew grammars (Wiktionary has no etymology for this entry)

funFacts: The double n (šadda) is what distinguishes هُنَّ (they, f.) from هُنَا (here).
pitfalls: The verb after هُنَّ ends in -na: هُنَّ يَأْكُلْنَ، يَشْرَبْنَ — the 2nd person “you (women)” has the same ending: تَأْكُلْنَ.
Only for a group made up entirely of women; one man in the group → هُمْ.
subtleties: Most spoken dialects have lost the feminine plural and say هُمْ for women too; Modern Standard Arabic requires هُنَّ.

profile.feeling: The invisible verb: absent in the present, essential for past and future.

senses.def: to be (past and future; the present “is” is not expressed)
auxiliary: كَانَ + present verb = past continuous or habit (“was doing, used to do”)
to exist, to be; there was (Wiktionary: “to exist, to be, there be”)

examples.tr: I will be at home tomorrow.
She was eating when I arrived.

examples.text: كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ، فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ…
examples.tr: Once upon a time, long, long ago…

collocations.tr: I had (lit. there was at me)

phrases.text: كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ، فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ
phrases.tr: there was, or there was not, in the old days
phrases.meaning: the traditional opening of a fairy tale: once upon a time

profile.synonymsNone: No real synonym. Its “sisters” (أَخَوَاتُ كَانَ: أَصْبَحَ “to become”, صَارَ “to become”, ظَلَّ “to remain”, لَيْسَ “not to be”) work the same way but add a meaning.

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *kawan- (“to be or exist in a place”); root ك و ن, verbal noun كَوْن (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Arab fairy tales start with كَانَ يَا مَا كَانَ — “once upon a time”.
The same root gives مَكَان (place) and كَوْن (being; the universe).
pitfalls: No verb “to be” in the present: هُوَ طَبِيبٌ = he is a doctor. Never *هُوَ يَكُونُ طَبِيبٌ for a simple “is”.
Its predicate is accusative: الْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ → كَانَ الْجَوُّ جَمِيلًا.
Hollow verb: the long ā shortens before consonant endings — كَانَ but كُنْتُ (I was), كُنَّا (we were).
subtleties: The present forms (يَكُونُ …) do exist: for the future (سَيَكُونُ), for habits and general truths, and after أَنْ (يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ = he must be).

profile.feeling: Everywhere: Arabic links clauses with وَ far more than English uses “and”.

examples.tr: My brother and I are at home.

collocations.tr: and so on, and so forth

synonyms.nuance: and then, afterwards — sequence with a gap in time
and so, and then — immediate sequence or consequence

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *wa; cognate with Hebrew וְ־ (ve-).

funFacts: Hebrew וְ (ve-) is the same Semitic word and is also written joined to the next word.
pitfalls: وَ is never written alone: it joins the next word — وَالْبَصَلُ، وَأَنَا.
In lists Arabic repeats وَ before every item: جَزَرٌ وَبَصَلٌ وَثُومٌ.
subtleties: Before al- the connecting hamza is silent: وَالْبَصَلُ = wa-l-baṣalu.
Arabic prose often begins sentences with وَ; translating every one as “and” sounds odd in English.

profile.feeling: An adult man; said with emphasis (كُنْ رَجُلًا!) it praises courage and reliability.

senses.def: a real man — brave, reliable (in praise or as a demand)

examples.tr: I saw a man in the street.
Two men and a woman came in.

phrases.meaning: a man is judged by how he acts when it matters

synonyms.nuance: gentleman; Mr. (as a title: السَّيِّدُ …)
a young man
male (sex), also of animals — not a polite word for a man

etymology.text: Originally “walker”: Wiktionary notes the meaning “foot-soldier” attested in Safaitic rgl. The same root ر ج ل gives رِجْل “leg, foot” (Proto-Semitic *rigl-), cognate with Hebrew רֶגֶל (regel, “foot”).

funFacts: In Gulf Arabic the word became رَيَّال (rayyāl) — j turns into y in many Gulf dialects (Wiktionary lists the Gulf forms).
Hebrew רֶגֶל (regel, foot) comes from the same root: a man was “one who goes on foot”.
pitfalls: Unvocalized رجل can be رَجُل (rajul, man) or رِجْل (rijl, leg): only the vowels or the context tell you.
The plural is broken: رِجَال — never *رَجُلُونَ.
subtleties: رِجَال also means “the men of a field”: رِجَالُ الْأَعْمَالِ (businessmen), رِجَالُ الدِّينِ (clergy).

profile.feeling: The standard, respectful word for a woman; with the article also “woman” as such, in general.

examples.tr: the wife of al-ʿAzīz (Potiphar’s wife, in the story of Joseph)

synonyms.nuance: lady; Mrs. — the polite word
female (sex), also of animals
wife — the usual word in that sense

etymology.text: Root م ر ء, as in مَرْء / اِمْرُؤ (“a man, a person”). The plural نِسَاء is built on another root; Wiktionary compares it to Hebrew נָשִׁים (nashím, “women”).

funFacts: The plural has nothing in common with the singular: اِمْرَأَة → نِسَاء, like English person → people.
Hebrew נָשִׁים (nashím, women) matches the Arabic plural نِسَاء.
pitfalls: With the article the first alif disappears: الْمَرْأَةُ (al-marʾa), not *الِامْرَأَةُ.
The first vowel is a connecting hamza: inside a sentence it is not pronounced and the kasra is not written — وَامْرَأَةٌ (wa-mraʾatun).
subtleties: الْمَرْأَةُ is often “woman” as a category: حُقُوقُ الْمَرْأَةِ = women’s rights.

profile.feeling: The everyday “boy”; in the plural, often simply “the kids”.

senses.def: child, offspring (son or daughter of any age)

examples.tr: The children are playing in the garden.

phrases.tr: the son is his father’s secret

synonyms.nuance: boy, lad — more literary
son (as a relative); وَلَد is broader

etymology.text: Root و ل د (“to give birth”). Wiktionary compares Hebrew יֶלֶד (yéled) and Geʿez ወልድ (wäld).

funFacts: Turkish evlat (child, offspring) comes from the plural أَوْلَاد (Wiktionary).
Hebrew יֶלֶד (yéled, boy, child) is the same Semitic word: an Arabic root that starts with w- often starts with y- in Hebrew.
pitfalls: أَوْلَاد often means “children” of both sexes: عِنْدِي ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْلَادٍ can include daughters.
Do not confuse وَلَد (walad, boy) with the verb وُلِدَ (wulida, he was born).
subtleties: In MSA writing صَبِيّ and غُلَام sound more literary; وَلَد is the word you hear every day.

profile.feeling: The everyday “girl”; within a family it is “daughter”.

synonyms.nuance: girl, young woman — more formal or literary
daughter — the more formal word in that sense

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *bint-: the feminine suffix *-t added to *bin- of اِبْن (ibn, “son”). Cognate with Hebrew בַּת (bat).

funFacts: Hebrew בַּת (bat, daughter) is the same word, with the n assimilated: *bint → bat.
English slang “bint” (a woman — derogatory, British) was borrowed from Arabic بِنْت (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: بِنْت ends in a plain ت, not ة — but it is feminine, and its plural is بَنَات.
In a family context بِنْتِي is “my daughter”, not “my girl”.
subtleties: In names بِنْت means “daughter of”: فَاطِمَةُ بِنْتُ مُحَمَّدٍ — the female counterpart of اِبْن / بْن.

profile.feeling: A child as a young human being — tender, small, to be protected.

senses.def: child (a minor, from a baby to about 12)

examples.tr: He was playing with the children.

synonyms.nuance: child in the sense of son or daughter; also “boy”
a baby that is still nursing

etymology.text: Root ط ف ل; Wiktionary gives no older origin. The word passed into Persian, Urdu and Ottoman Turkish (Turkish tıfıl) and Maltese (tifel, “boy”).

funFacts: Maltese tifel means “boy” — the same Arabic word (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: طِفْل is grammatically masculine but can mean a girl too; for a girl you also hear طِفْلَة.
The plural starts with a hamza: أَطْفَال, الْأَطْفَالُ.
subtleties: طِفْل stresses age (a minor); وَلَد stresses birth and family (someone’s child) or means “boy”.

profile.feeling: A neutral “person, individual” — the word for counting people.

senses.def: figure, shape (seen from afar); a character

examples.tr: There are five people in the room.
I saw a figure in the distance.

synonyms.nuance: a human being — stresses humanity, not the individual
an individual; a member (of a family, a group)

etymology.text: Root ش خ ص (“to rise, to appear”); Wiktionary gives no older origin. It passed into Persian and Ottoman Turkish: Turkish şahıs “person”.

funFacts: Turkish şahıs (person) — and Azerbaijani şəxs, Uzbek shaxs — come from شَخْص (Wiktionary).
شَخْصِيَّة (personality; a character in a story) is شَخْص + -iyya, like English person → personality.
pitfalls: To count people Arabic uses أَشْخَاص, not نَاس: ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْخَاصٍ = three people.
شَخْص stays masculine even for a woman: هِيَ شَخْصٌ طَيِّبٌ (she is a kind person).
subtleties: In law شَخْصٌ اعْتِبَارِيٌّ is a legal person (a company, an institution).

profile.feeling: People in general — “folks”, what “people say”.

examples.tr: There are many people in the market.

phrases.tr: people follow the religion of their kings
phrases.meaning: people follow the example of those who rule them

synonyms.nuance: people, some people — literary; can be indefinite: أُنَاسٌ كَثِيرُونَ
a people, a nation — not “people” in general
persons — the word for counting

etymology.text: Back-formation from النَّاس (an-nās), a contraction of الْأُنَاس (al-ʔunās). Cognate with Aramaic אֲנָשָׁא (ʾănāšā) and Biblical Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ (ʾĕnōš, “man, mankind”).

funFacts: The last sura of the Qurʾān is سُورَةُ النَّاسِ, “Mankind”.
Biblical Hebrew אֱנוֹשׁ (enosh, mankind) — also the name Enos — is related (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: نَاس is plural: النَّاسُ يَقُولُونَ (people say), not *يَقُولُ — and النَّاسُ طَيِّبُونَ, not *طَيِّبٌ.
It is nearly always used with the article: النَّاسُ = people in general.
subtleties: A counted number of people is أَشْخَاص: ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْخَاصٍ — not *ثَلَاثَةُ نَاسٍ.

profile.feeling: Warm and loyal — the root is “truth”: a friend is someone true to you.

examples.tr: I have many friends in Egypt.

phrases.meaning: choose your companion before you set out

phrases.tr: the friend in the time of hardship
phrases.meaning: a friend in need is a friend indeed

synonyms.nuance: companion, friend — very common in speech; also “owner”
companion, comrade (on a journey, in a party)
colleague, classmate — a friend from work or school

etymology.text: From the root ص د ق (“truth, sincerity”: صِدْق “truth”); Wiktionary gives no older origin. The masculine plural أَصْدِقَاء and the rarer صُدَقَاء are both listed.

funFacts: Turkish sadık (loyal) comes from صَادِق (truthful), of the same root.
Hebrew צֶדֶק (tsédek, justice) belongs to the cognate root צ ד ק.
pitfalls: The masculine plural أَصْدِقَاءُ is a diptote: no tanwīn (not *أَصْدِقَاءٌ), and -a in the indefinite genitive.
صَدِيقَة can mean “girlfriend” in a romantic sense, depending on the context.
subtleties: Do not confuse صَدِيق (ṣadīq, friend) with صِدِّيق (ṣiddīq, always truthful — the epithet of Abū Bakr).

profile.feeling: A learner at school or university — literally “one who seeks” (knowledge).

senses.def: seeker, one who asks for something; applicant

examples.tr: I am a student at the university.
He is a seeker of knowledge.

phrases.meaning: go as far as you must in order to learn (a famous saying; its attribution to the Prophet is considered weak)

synonyms.nuance: pupil — a younger school learner; also disciple
one who studies a subject

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of طَلَبَ (ṭalaba, “to seek, to ask for”).

funFacts: “Taliban” is the Pashto plural of طَالِب — “students” (of religion); Wiktionary lists Pashto طالب.
Turkish talebe (student) comes from another Arabic plural of the word, طَلَبَة (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: There are three plurals: طُلَّاب (the usual one), طَلَبَة (also common), طَالِبُونَ (rare for students). Learn طُلَّاب.
A female student is طَالِبَة (plural طَالِبَات); a mixed group is طُلَّاب.
subtleties: The word is a participle: “one who seeks”. Arabic sees a student as a seeker — hence the saying about China.

profile.feeling: A respected figure: “the one who makes (others) know”.

senses.def: master of a trade; boss (in a workshop)

examples.tr: The teacher is in the classroom.

phrases.text: قُمْ لِلْمُعَلِّمِ وَفِّهِ التَّبْجِيلَا، كَادَ الْمُعَلِّمُ أَنْ يَكُونَ رَسُولَا
phrases.tr: Stand up for the teacher and give him full respect: the teacher is almost a messenger (prophet).

synonyms.nuance: teacher, especially at secondary school; very common in Egypt
professor, teacher; also a polite title for educated men (“Mr.”)

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of the verb عَلَّمَ (ʿallama, “to teach”), root ع ل م (“knowledge”).

funFacts: Turkish muallim and Swahili mwalimu (teacher) come from مُعَلِّم (Wiktionary).
The same root gives عِلْم (knowledge, science), عَالِم (scholar) and عَالَم (world).
pitfalls: مُعَلِّم (muʿallim, teacher) vs مُتَعَلِّم (mutaʿallim, learner; educated) — two letters make the opposite.
The masculine plural is sound: مُعَلِّمُونَ (nominative), مُعَلِّمِينَ (accusative and genitive); feminine مُعَلِّمَات.
subtleties: In Egypt and the Levant the spoken word مْعَلِّم / مِعَلِّم is also a respectful title for a master craftsman or a boss.

absent.reason: Arabic has no neuter and no word for “it”: every thing is masculine or feminine, and a pronoun that refers to it takes its gender.
absent.use: هُوَ for a masculine thing (الْبَابُ؟ هُوَ هُنَا — the door? it is here), هِيَ for a feminine thing and for any non-human plural (الْغُرْفَةُ؟ هِيَ هُنَاكَ; الْكُتُبُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا).

absent.reason: No separate word: the definite article al- (الْ) is written joined to the noun and is part of the noun’s forms (the DEF cells). Before the 14 sun letters its l is assimilated: الشَّقَّةُ (aš-šaqqa), not al-šaqqa.
absent.use: الْ + noun (the DEF forms): الْبَيْتُ، الْغُرْفَةُ، الشَّقَّةُ

absent.reason: No indefinite article: an indefinite noun ends in nunation (tanwīn: -un, -an, -in); diptotes (نَوَافِذُ، مَصَابِيحُ) are indefinite without it.
absent.use: the noun with tanwīn (the INDF forms): بَيْتٌ = a house, غُرْفَةٌ = a room
